title: The Transformer Block
oneLineScope: Residual connections, layer norm, and the position-wise FFN — the repeating unit.
prose:
Where we are. The previous two nodes handed us the pieces that let a position read its neighbors: multi-head self-attention, which lets every position gather a content-weighted mixture of the others, and the positional encoding that tells it where in the sequence everything sits. What we do not yet have is a unit we can stack. Attention mixes information across tokens, but layer for layer it is a linear projection followed by a convex average — it moves information sideways without doing much nonlinear computation on what arrives. And a single round of mixing, however many heads, is shallow.

The gist. The transformer block is the repeating unit of the architecture — the brick everything is built from. Each block has two parts: a self-attention sublayer that lets each token gather context from the rest of the sequence, and a position-wise feed-forward network that does private nonlinear computation on each token afterward. Each of those two parts is wrapped in the same protective packaging — a residual (skip) connection and a layer normalization — so that many blocks can be stacked deep without the training collapsing. Mix across, then compute within, and do it safely enough to repeat.

Why it matters. Depth is where transformers get their power, and a layer you cannot stack is useless. This block is precisely the unit you can stack: each sublayer preserves its input’s shape and adds only a correction to it, so blocks compose cleanly to any depth. The full transformer is nothing more than \(L\) identical copies of this brick with input and output plumbing bolted on.

Two sublayers: mix across, then compute within

A block has exactly two sublayers, in order. The first is the multi-head self-attention you already know — the cross-token step, where each position pulls in information from the rest of the sequence. The second is a position-wise feed-forward network (FFN): a small nonlinear network applied independently and identically to each position's vector, with no communication between positions. The division of labor is the thing to hold onto. Attention is the only place tokens talk to each other; the FFN is where each token, having gathered its context, does private nonlinear work on it. Mix across, then compute within — and because the block is stacked, the next block's attention then mixes the results of this block's per-token computation, and so on. Depth alternates between the two.

The feed-forward network

The FFN is the most ordinary object in the architecture, and after attention it is almost a relief: it is a two-layer fully connected network with a single nonlinearity, exactly the kind of multilayer perceptron you have known for decades. The intuition is plain — once attention has decided which information a token should hold, the FFN is where the token sits down and does something with it. Acting on one position's vector \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}\) (a single row of the hidden state),

\[ \operatorname{FFN}(x) = \max(0,\, x W_1 + b_1)\, W_2 + b_2 \]

The first linear layer has weight \(W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{ff}}}\) and bias \(b_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}}\); it projects the vector up to a wider inner dimension \(d_{\text{ff}}\). The \(\max(0,\cdot)\) is the ReLU, applied elementwise — the one source of nonlinearity. The second linear layer, \(W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}} \times d_{\text{model}}}\) with bias \(b_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}\), projects back down to the model width, so the FFN is shape-preserving: \(d_{\text{model}}\) in, \(d_{\text{model}}\) out. In the base model \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\) and \(d_{\text{ff}} = 2048\) — a fourfold expansion in the middle. The expand-then-project shape is what gives a single position room to compute: the ReLU carves the wide \(d_{\text{ff}}\)-dimensional space into many linear regions, and the model uses that width as scratch space before squeezing the result back to \(d_{\text{model}}\).

“Position-wise” is the word that matters. The same weights \(W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2\) are applied to every position — it is one small network, shared, run \(n\) times in parallel, once per row of the \(n \times d_{\text{model}}\) hidden state. It is the per-token nonlinear computation sitting between attention's bouts of cross-token mixing. (Two readings amount to the same thing: an FFN run independently on each of the \(n\) rows, or a pair of \(1\times1\) convolutions over the sequence. They compute the identical function.)

It is worth pausing on why attention needs the FFN beside it at all. A self-attention sublayer, for all its expressiveness in choosing whom to read, applies only linear projections and a convex average to the values it gathers; stack two attention layers with nothing between them and the composition stays close to linear in the values. The FFN supplies the missing ingredient — a genuine pointwise nonlinearity with its own wide hidden space — so that the two sublayers together can express functions neither could alone. The clean reading of the alternation is this: attention decides what information each token should have, and the FFN decides what to make of it. Counting parameters underscores how much of the model lives here: with \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\) and \(d_{\text{ff}} = 2048\), the FFN's two weight matrices hold about \(2 \times 512 \times 2048 \approx 2.1\) million parameters per block — typically the larger share of a block's weights, more than the attention projections.

Around each sublayer: residual + layer norm

Stacking nonlinear layers deep is exactly the regime that, in the connectionist nets you knew, made gradients vanish or explode — the signal degrades as it propagates back through many layers. Two devices, applied around each of the two sublayers, keep a deep stack trainable.

The first is the residual connection — the same skip connection from the residual networks (ResNets) that made very deep image models trainable a year before. Instead of replacing its input, a sublayer adds to it: the input is carried forward unchanged on an identity path and the sublayer's output is added on top. If \(\operatorname{Sublayer}(\cdot)\) is either attention or the FFN, the contribution is \(x + \operatorname{Sublayer}(x)\). The point is the identity path: in the backward pass, the gradient reaches earlier layers directly along the skip, without being repeatedly multiplied by the sublayer's Jacobian, so it neither vanishes nor explodes through depth. The sublayer only has to learn a correction to its input rather than a full re-representation. This stream of summed contributions — what later writers call the residual stream — is why every sublayer is built to be shape-preserving (\(d_{\text{model}}\) in, \(d_{\text{model}}\) out): so that adding to it is well defined.

The second is layer normalization (Ba, Kiros & Hinton, 2016). For one position's vector, it computes the mean and variance across that vector's own \(d_{\text{model}}\) features, normalizes the vector to zero mean and unit variance, then rescales and shifts by two learned per-feature parameters \(\gamma, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}\). The contrast with batch normalization is the point worth dwelling on, since you may reach for batch norm first. Batch norm normalizes each feature across the examples in a minibatch — it couples the examples together and depends on batch statistics. Layer norm normalizes each example across its own features, so it touches one token at a time and is completely independent of the other tokens in the sequence or the batch. For variable-length sequences batched together that independence is exactly what you want: a token's normalization must not depend on how many other tokens happen to share its batch, nor on padding. Layer norm sidesteps all of that.

The learned \(\gamma, \beta\) matter: without them, forcing every vector to unit variance would throw away scale information the network may need, so the normalization sets a clean, optimizer-friendly distribution and then lets the model learn back whatever scale and shift each feature should carry.

In the original transformer the two combine in the post-LN arrangement — normalize after the residual add:

\[ \operatorname{output} = \operatorname{LayerNorm}\!\left(x + \operatorname{Sublayer}(x)\right) \]

applied once around attention and once around the FFN. So a full block, reading top to bottom, is: \(x \to \operatorname{LayerNorm}(x + \operatorname{SelfAttention}(x)) \to \operatorname{LayerNorm}(\cdot + \operatorname{FFN}(\cdot))\), each arrow preserving the \(n \times d_{\text{model}}\) shape.

The subtlety: post-LN vs. pre-LN

The placement of that LayerNorm — after the add, as published — turns out to be the awkward choice for very deep models. With post-LN the normalization sits on the residual path, so the clean identity route that residuals were meant to provide is interrupted at every block; training deep post-LN transformers from scratch needs a careful learning-rate warmup or it diverges. The widely adopted refinement, analyzed by Xiong et al. (2020), is pre-LN: normalize the input to each sublayer instead, \(x + \operatorname{Sublayer}(\operatorname{LayerNorm}(x))\). Now the residual stream runs from input to output unnormalized and unbroken, gradients are far better behaved at depth, and the warmup becomes optional. This is a well-established later improvement, not part of the 2017 design — most large models since adopt some pre-LN variant, but the original paper, and the diagram below, are post-LN. Keep the distinction straight; it is a common source of confusion when reading code against the paper.

Where it connects

This block is the unit of depth. The full transformer stacks \(L\) of them (the base model uses \(L = 6\) per stack) and adds the input and output plumbing; the decoder variant of the block grows a third sublayer for cross-attention, but the residual-plus-LayerNorm wrapping is identical. The training behavior these devices were built to protect — the warmup schedule that post-LN demands, how the residual stream interacts with the optimizer — is the subject of optimization and training dynamics.

diagrams.caption: One transformer block: two sublayers (self-attention, then FFN), each wrapped in a residual skip and layer normalization. Shown in the original post-LN arrangement.
diagrams.altText: A top-to-bottom diagram of one transformer block. The input X (shape n by d_model) flows down into a multi-head self-attention box; its output meets an Add and Norm box that computes LayerNorm of the input plus the sublayer output. A green residual skip connection arcs around the attention sublayer from the input into the Add and Norm. That result (still n by d_model) flows into a position-wise feed-forward (FFN) box, followed by a second Add and Norm with its own residual skip around it, producing the block output (n by d_model). A dashed enclosure marks that L such blocks are stacked. Margin notes mark that attention mixes across tokens while the FFN is per-token and independent.
diagrams.prompt: Structural diagram, top to bottom, of a single transformer block in the original post-LN arrangement. At the top, an input matrix labeled X with shape n by d_model. An arrow leads down into a box labeled 'multi-head self-attention'. Its output leads into a box labeled 'Add & Norm' annotated 'LayerNorm(x + sublayer)'. A residual skip connection arcs from the input X around the self-attention box directly into that Add & Norm box; label it 'residual (skip)'. The Add & Norm output (shape n by d_model) leads down into a box labeled 'position-wise feed-forward (FFN)', whose output leads into a second 'Add & Norm' box, again with a residual skip arcing around the FFN from its input; label this skip 'residual (skip)' as well. The second Add & Norm produces the 'block output' with shape n by d_model at the bottom. Draw a light dashed enclosure around the whole block annotated 'x L blocks' to indicate the block is stacked L times. Add a small margin note pointing at the attention box reading 'mixes across tokens' and one pointing at the FFN box reading 'per-token, independent'. Label the n by d_model shape at the input, between the sublayers, and at the output. Structural diagram: the two sublayers, the two residual skips, and the post-LN ordering must be exact.

diagrams.caption: The position-wise feed-forward network: expand d_model to d_ff, apply ReLU, project back to d_model — the same weights applied independently at every position.
diagrams.altText: A left-to-right diagram of the position-wise feed-forward network applied to one token. An input vector x of width d_model (512) enters the first linear layer, x W1 + b1, expanding it to a wider hidden vector of width d_ff (2048). The hidden vector passes through a ReLU, max of zero and the input, then through a second linear layer, h W2 + b2, projecting back down to width d_model (512), giving the output vector y. A note states that the same weights W1, b1, W2, b2 are applied independently and identically at every position, with no mixing across tokens.
diagrams.prompt: Structural data-flow diagram, left to right, of the position-wise feed-forward network applied to one token. On the left, an input vector labeled x drawn as a tall thin rectangle, annotated with width d_model (= 512). An arrow leads into a box labeled 'Linear 1' annotated 'x W1 + b1', which produces a taller hidden vector labeled h, annotated with width d_ff (= 2048) to show it is wider; add a small note 'expand 512 to 2048'. An arrow leads from the hidden vector into a box labeled 'ReLU' annotated 'max(0, .)'. An arrow leads into a box labeled 'Linear 2' annotated 'h W2 + b2', annotated 'project back 2048 to 512', producing an output vector labeled y on the right with width d_model (= 512). Below the whole pipeline, a note reads: 'same weights W1, b1, W2, b2 applied independently at every position — no mixing across tokens'. Emphasize the widening in the middle (d_model to d_ff) and the narrowing back. Structural diagram: the up-projection to d_ff, the ReLU, and the down-projection to d_model must be exact, with shapes labeled.

bibliography.citation: Vaswani, A., et al. (2017). "Attention Is All You Need." NeurIPS.
bibliography.annotation: The defining source for the block. §3.1 describes the encoder/decoder sublayers and the 'LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))' residual wrapping; §3.3 specifies the position-wise FFN, including d_model = 512 and d_ff = 2048. Read these two short subsections for the exact structure.

bibliography.citation: Ba, J. L., Kiros, J. R., & Hinton, G. E. (2016). "Layer Normalization." arXiv:1607.06450.
bibliography.annotation: Introduces layer normalization. §3 gives the per-example, across-features statistics and the contrast with batch normalization; the motivation for sequence models and RNNs (no dependence on batch or sequence length) is exactly why the transformer uses it.

bibliography.citation: Xiong, R., et al. (2020). "On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture." ICML.
bibliography.annotation: The pre-LN vs. post-LN analysis, and the source for the subtlety in this node. Shows why post-LN needs learning-rate warmup and why moving LayerNorm to each sublayer's input (pre-LN) keeps gradients well-behaved at depth. Read for the attributed later refinement only — it is not the 2017 design.

bibliography.citation: Rush, A., et al. "The Annotated Transformer."
bibliography.annotation: A line-by-line PyTorch reimplementation of the paper. The SublayerConnection and LayerNorm classes make the residual-plus-norm wrapping concrete; the PositionwiseFeedForward class is the FFN in five lines. Best read alongside §3 of Vaswani et al.
